relationship: parallel opened heavens and sight of divine glory
rationale: Ezekiel sees God's visions when the heavens open during captivity by Chebar. Stephen likewise sees the heavens opened and God's glory, there with Jesus standing at God's right hand; the witnesses and settings differ.
source_text: And it happened in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth of the month, while I was among the captives by the River Chebar: the heavens opened, and I saw visions of God.

target_units.text: But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at God’s right hand.
He said, “Look, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand.”

relationship: related dating of Ezekiel's visions by captivity years
rationale: The opening dates the vision to the fifth year of King Jehoiakim's captivity. Ezekiel 40 dates a later vision to the twenty-fifth year of our captivity and fourteenth after the city's capture, connecting the book's chronology through captivity while preserving its differing dates and native royal name.
source_text: On the fifth of the month—this was the fifth year of King Jehoiakim’s captivity—

target_units.text: In the twenty-fifth year of our captivity, in the first month, on the tenth of the month, in the fourteenth year after the city was captured, on that day the Lord’s hand came upon me, and He led me
in a vision of God into Israel’s land and set me upon a very high mountain. Upon it, opposite, was something like a city’s structure.

relationship: repeated Lord's hand and speech upon Ezekiel
rationale: The Lord's word comes to Ezekiel at Chebar and His hand comes upon the speaker. Ezekiel 3 again reports the Lord's hand upon him together with a spoken direction, there sending him to the plain.
source_text: the Lord’s word came to Ezekiel son of Buzi, the priest, in the land of the Chaldeans by the River Chebar; and the Lord’s hand came upon me,

target_units.text: The Lord’s hand came upon me, and He said to me, “Rise and go out to the plain, and you will be spoken to there.”

relationship: shared wind, cloud, fire and lightning imagery of divine manifestation
rationale: Ezekiel's vision begins with a sweeping wind, cloud, brightness and flashing fire. The psalm likewise portrays God's coming with wind, clouds, radiance, fiery coals and lightning; it does not repeat the origin from the north or electrum appearance.
source_text: and I looked, and behold, a sweeping wind was coming from the north, and a great cloud was within it, with brightness around it and fire flashing like lightning; within it was something like the appearance of electrum, within the fire, and brightness within it.

target_units.text: Smoke rose in His anger, and fire from His face set things ablaze; coals were kindled from Him.
And He bent heaven and came down, and gloom was beneath His feet.
And He mounted cherubim and flew; He flew on the wings of winds.
And He made darkness His hiding place; His tent was around Him, dark water in clouds of the air.
From the far-shining radiance before Him, the clouds passed— hail and coals of fire.
And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave His voice.
And He sent out arrows and scattered them; He multiplied lightning flashes and threw them into turmoil.

relationship: later explicit identification of the Chebar living creature
rationale: Ezekiel first sees four living creatures with a human likeness. The later vision expressly identifies the living creature seen beneath Israel's God at Chebar as cherubim, supplying the book's own identification rather than an identification from another vision tradition.
source_text: And within it was something like a likeness of four living creatures. This was their appearance: a human likeness was upon them,

target_units.text: This is the living creature I had seen beneath the God of Israel at the river Chebar, and I knew that it was cherubim.

relationship: repeated four faces with differing native wing counts
rationale: Both accounts assign four faces to each creature. This unit gives each four wings, while Ezekiel 10:21 gives each eight wings and adds human hands beneath them; the relationship preserves rather than normalizes that difference.
source_text: and each had four faces, and each had four wings.

target_units.text: Each had four faces, each had eight wings, and the likeness of human hands was beneath their wings.

relationship: shared flashing-bronze appearance of visionary feet
rationale: Ezekiel describes winged feet with sparks like flashing bronze. Daniel's visionary figure likewise has arms and feet like flashing bronze; Daniel does not give those feet wings or reproduce Ezekiel's whole description.
source_text: Their legs were straight, and their feet were winged, with sparks like flashing bronze; and their wings were light.

target_units.text: His body was like a tarshish stone, his face like a flash of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and feet like flashing bronze, and the sound of his speech like the sound of an uproar.

relationship: repeated human-hand likeness beneath the creatures' wings
rationale: The Chebar description places a human hand beneath the wings. Ezekiel 10 explicitly describes the likeness of human hands beneath the cherubim's wings, repeating this unusual combination of human and winged features.
source_text: A human hand was beneath their wings on their four sides; and the faces of all four of them

target_units.text: I saw the cherubim, the likeness of human hands beneath their wings.

relationship: repeated straight-ahead movement of Chebar's creatures
rationale: The faces of all four do not turn as they walk, and each goes straight ahead. Ezekiel 10 explicitly recalls the faces seen at Chebar and likewise says each went straight ahead, linking the movement descriptions through the stated earlier vision.
source_text: did not turn as they walked; each went straight ahead.

target_units.text: As for the likeness of their faces, these are the faces I had seen beneath the glory of the God of Israel at the river Chebar; each of them went straight ahead.

relationship: later explicit recollection of the faces seen at Chebar
rationale: This unit describes the human, lion, calf and eagle faces in the Chebar vision. Ezekiel 10:22 explicitly identifies its faces with those seen beneath God's glory at Chebar, although that later unit does not repeat the four individual face names.
source_text: The likeness of their faces was a human face and a lion’s face on the right for all four, and a calf’s face on the left for all four, and an eagle’s face for all four.

target_units.text: As for the likeness of their faces, these are the faces I had seen beneath the glory of the God of Israel at the river Chebar; each of them went straight ahead.

relationship: related heavenly wings covering the creatures' bodies
rationale: Ezekiel's four-winged creatures have two wings joined and two covering their bodies' upper part. Isaiah's six-winged seraphim likewise use wings to cover themselves, there two for faces and two for feet, with another two for flying; the beings and arrangements are distinct.
source_text: The wings of all four were stretched out above; each had two joined to one another, and two covered the top of their bodies.

target_units.text: And seraphim stood around Him: each one had six wings, and each one had six wings; with two they covered their faces, and with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew.

relationship: same-chapter spirit and coordinated movement
rationale: The creatures follow where the spirit goes without turning. Ezekiel 1:20 locates the spirit for movement where the cloud is and explains creatures and wheels rising together through a spirit of life in the wheels, developing the coordination without dropping its cloud clause.
source_text: Each went straight ahead. Wherever the spirit was going, they went and did not turn.

target_units.text: Wherever the cloud was, there was the spirit for movement; the living creatures and the wheels went and rose together with them, because a spirit of life was in the wheels.

relationship: repeated burning coals among the living creatures or cherubim
rationale: The Chebar vision places burning coals and torch-like fire among the living creatures. Ezekiel 10 likewise locates burning coals among the cherubim and commands that they be taken and scattered over the city, adding a judgment action to the shared fiery setting.
source_text: And amid the living creatures was an appearance like burning coals of fire, like the sight of torches whirling among the living creatures, and brightness of the fire; lightning came out of the fire.

target_units.text: He said to the man wearing the robe, “Go in among the wheels beneath the cherubim, fill your hands with burning coals from among the cherubim, and scatter them over the city.” He went in before me.

relationship: related wheels adjoining the visionary creatures
rationale: Ezekiel first notices one wheel on the earth adjoining the four living creatures. The later vision describes four wheels, one beside each cherub, providing a more distributed arrangement without changing this unit's singular wording.
source_text: I looked, and behold, one wheel was on the earth adjoining the four living creatures;

target_units.text: I saw, and behold, four wheels stood beside the cherubim, one wheel beside one cherub. The wheels’ appearance was like the appearance of a carbuncle stone.

relationship: repeated common wheel appearance and wheel-within-wheel workmanship
rationale: Both descriptions say all four wheels share one likeness and compare their workmanship or appearance with a wheel within a wheel. The target does not repeat this unit's tharsis comparison.
source_text: the appearance of the wheels was like the appearance of tharsis, and all four had one likeness; their workmanship was as though a wheel were within a wheel.

target_units.text: Their appearance was one likeness for all four, as when a wheel is within a wheel.

relationship: repeated four-direction movement without turning
rationale: Both passages say the wheels move toward their four sides or directions without turning. Ezekiel 10 further explains that they follow wherever the leading part looks.
source_text: They went toward their four sides; they did not turn as they went,

target_units.text: As they went, they went toward their four directions; they did not turn as they went. For wherever the one leading part looked, they went, and they did not turn as they went.

relationship: repeated backs full of eyes all around
rationale: Ezekiel describes the backs of all four as full of eyes all around. The later account likewise includes their backs among the parts full of surrounding eyes, also naming hands, wings and wheels; neither explanation substitutes rims for the supplied backs.
source_text: nor did their backs; they were tall, and I saw them. The backs of all four were full of eyes all around.

target_units.text: Their backs, their hands, their wings, and the wheels were full of eyes all around, upon their four wheels.

relationship: repeated coordinated movement and rising of creatures and wheels
rationale: The wheels move beside the living creatures and rise when they rise. Ezekiel 10 likewise describes wheels accompanying the cherubim and rising with them, also adding their coordinated standing and the spirit of life.
source_text: When the living creatures went, the wheels moved beside them; when the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels rose.

target_units.text: When the cherubim went, the wheels went beside them. When the cherubim raised their wings to rise from the earth, their wheels did not turn.
When they stood, these stood; when they rose, these rose with them, because a spirit of life was in them.

relationship: repeated spirit of life explaining coordinated rising
rationale: Ezekiel 1 explains the creatures and wheels rising together through a spirit of life in the wheels, after naming the cloud and spirit for movement. Ezekiel 10 likewise explains coordinated rising through a spirit of life in them, without repeating the cloud clause.
source_text: Wherever the cloud was, there was the spirit for movement; the living creatures and the wheels went and rose together with them, because a spirit of life was in the wheels.

target_units.text: When they stood, these stood; when they rose, these rose with them, because a spirit of life was in them.

relationship: repeated movement, standing and rising together
rationale: Ezekiel lists the wheels' movement, standing and rising with the living creatures. The later cherubim account repeats these coordinated actions and the explanation that a spirit of life is in them.
source_text: When they went, these went; when they stood, these stood; when they rose from the earth, these rose together with them, because a spirit of life was in the wheels.

target_units.text: When the cherubim went, the wheels went beside them. When the cherubim raised their wings to rise from the earth, their wheels did not turn.
When they stood, these stood; when they rose, these rose with them, because a spirit of life was in them.

relationship: related firmament and luminous stone imagery in a divine vision
rationale: Ezekiel sees a crystal-like firmament above the creatures. Exodus describes the place beneath God's feet as sapphire brickwork resembling heaven's clear firmament; the shared visual vocabulary preserves the different materials and positions.
source_text: Above the living creatures’ heads was a likeness as of a firmament, like the appearance of crystal, stretched out above their wings;

target_units.text: and they saw the place where the God of Israel stood. What was beneath His feet was like sapphire brickwork, like the appearance of the firmament of heaven in its clarity.

relationship: same-chapter joined wings and bodily covering
rationale: Both descriptions mention joined wings and bodily covering. Ezekiel 1:11 distinguishes two joined wings from two covering the top of the bodies; Ezekiel 1:23 describes two joined together covering their bodies beneath the firmament, preserving the different descriptions.
source_text: and beneath the firmament their wings were stretched out, fluttering one toward another; each had two joined together, covering their bodies.

target_units.text: The wings of all four were stretched out above; each had two joined to one another, and two covered the top of their bodies.

relationship: repeated audible sound of the creatures' wings
rationale: Ezekiel hears the wings like much water as the creatures move. In the later vision the cherubim's wings are heard as far as the outer court, there compared with God Shaddai's speaking voice rather than water.
source_text: As they went, I heard the sound of their wings like the sound of much water; when they stood, their wings came to rest.

target_units.text: The sound of the cherubim’s wings was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God Shaddai speaking.

relationship: related speech within the vision above the cherubim
rationale: A voice comes from above the firmament over the creatures' heads. Ezekiel 10 again presents the throne above the firmament over the cherubim and then records a spoken command to the robed man, connecting speech with that repeated visionary setting.
source_text: And behold, a voice came from above the firmament that was over their heads.

target_units.text: I saw, and behold, above the firmament over the cherubim’s head was something like sapphire stone, a throne’s likeness above them.
He said to the man wearing the robe, “Go in among the wheels beneath the cherubim, fill your hands with burning coals from among the cherubim, and scatter them over the city.” He went in before me.

relationship: repeated sapphire-like throne above the firmament
rationale: Ezekiel describes a sapphire-like throne above the firmament, with a human-like form above it. Ezekiel 10 repeats the sapphire stone and throne likeness above the cherubim's firmament, without repeating the human-form clause in that unit.
source_text: Like the appearance of a sapphire stone was the likeness of a throne upon it; and above the likeness of the throne was a likeness like the form of a human being.

target_units.text: I saw, and behold, above the firmament over the cherubim’s head was something like sapphire stone, a throne’s likeness above them.

relationship: repeated electrum above the waist and fire below
rationale: The visionary appearance is electrum-like from the waist upward and fire-like below. Ezekiel 8 repeats the likeness of a man with electrum above the waist and fire below, a close correspondence in material and bodily division.
source_text: I saw something like the sight of electrum from the appearance of a waist upward; and from the appearance of a waist down below I saw something like the appearance of fire, with its brightness all around.

target_units.text: and I saw, and behold, the likeness of a man: from His waist downward, fire, and from His waist upward, like the appearance of electrum.

relationship: shared bow-in-cloud appearance with different stated functions
rationale: Ezekiel compares the surrounding brightness of the Lord's glory with a bow in a rainy cloud. Genesis describes God's bow appearing in the cloud as a covenant sign; the visual counterpart does not make Ezekiel's unit explicitly restate that covenant.
source_text: Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a rainy day, so was the arrangement of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of the Lord’s glory. I saw it, and I fall upon my face, and I heard the voice of One speaking.

target_units.text: I set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth.
“And when I gather clouds over the earth, My bow shall appear in the cloud.
And I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of all flesh; and the waters shall never again become a flood to blot out all flesh.
“My bow shall be in the cloud, and I will look upon it and remember the everlasting covenant between Me and every living creature of all flesh upon the earth.”

relationship: related prostration and speech in a visionary encounter
rationale: Ezekiel falls upon his face after seeing the Lord's glory and hears a speaking voice. Daniel likewise reports falling face down before being raised to hear commands, but says he initially did not hear the speech; the auditory sequence is preserved.
source_text: Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a rainy day, so was the arrangement of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of the Lord’s glory. I saw it, and I fall upon my face, and I heard the voice of One speaking.

target_units.text: I did not hear the sound of his speech; I had fallen face down upon the earth.
He brought a hand toward me and raised me upon my knees, upon the soles of my feet.

He said to me, “Daniel, you are a man worthy of pity. Understand the commands I speak to you, and stand in your place, for I have just been sent to you.” As he spoke this command with me, I stood trembling.

relationship: parallel commissioning command to stand on one's feet
rationale: Ezekiel is commanded to stand on his feet so that he may hear the speaker. In the Damascus-road account Jesus likewise commands Saul to rise and stand on his feet before appointing him a servant and witness, a particular commissioning posture in another encounter.
source_text: He said to me, “Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak to you.”

target_units.text: But rise and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you a servant and witness of the things in which you have seen Me and those in which I will appear to you,

relationship: related raising of a vision recipient to receive speech
rationale: A spirit raises Ezekiel and sets him on his feet as he hears the speaker. Daniel is likewise raised by an approaching hand and commanded to stand and understand the words, preserving the hand's action rather than calling it a spirit in Daniel.
source_text: A spirit came upon me, took me up, raised me, and set me on my feet; I heard Him speaking to me,

target_units.text: He brought a hand toward me and raised me upon my knees, upon the soles of my feet.

He said to me, “Daniel, you are a man worthy of pity. Understand the commands I speak to you, and stand in your place, for I have just been sent to you.” As he spoke this command with me, I stood trembling.

relationship: parallel prophetic sending to a resistant people
rationale: Ezekiel is sent to Israel's house, described as embittering God across generations. Isaiah is likewise sent to a people whose heart, hearing and sight are unresponsive, connecting prophetic commission with resistant recipients while retaining each diagnosis.
source_text: and He said to me, “Son of man, I am sending you out to the house of Israel, those who embitter Me, who have embittered Me, they and their fathers, until this present day,

target_units.text: And I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And I said, Behold, here I am; send me.
And He said, Go, and say to this people: Hearing, you will hear and certainly not understand; and seeing, you will see and certainly not perceive.

For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I will heal them.

relationship: repeated recognition that a prophet was among them
rationale: Ezekiel's commission says the people will know that a prophet is among them, with the condition worded as listening or being terrified. Ezekiel 33 likewise predicts their recognition that a prophet was among them when the announced event arrives.
source_text: If indeed they listen or are terrified—for it is an embittering house—they will know that you are a prophet among them.

target_units.text: When it comes, they will say, ‘Behold, it has arrived,’ and know that a prophet was among them.”

relationship: parallel assurance against fear amid prophetic opposition
rationale: Ezekiel must not fear the people's words or faces despite their surrounding hostility. Jeremiah likewise must rise, speak the commanded words and not fear his opponents, with assurance that their fighting will not prevail.
source_text: And you, son of man, do not fear them or be shaken before their faces, because they will rage and gather against you all around, and you dwell among scorpions. Do not fear their words or be shaken before their faces, for it is an embittering house.

target_units.text: But you, gird your waist, rise and tell them everything I command you. Do not fear them or be terrified before them, because I am with you to rescue you, says the Lord.
Behold, on this day I have made you like a fortified city and like a strong bronze wall against all Judah’s kings, its rulers and the people of the land,
and they will fight you, but they will certainly not prevail against you, because I am with you to rescue you, said the Lord.

relationship: related command to deliver divine words despite uncertain response
rationale: Ezekiel must speak God's words, if indeed the people listen or are terrified. Jeremiah likewise must deliver all commanded words without subtraction, with the possibility that hearers may turn from evil; the response clauses differ and are not rewritten as a shared refusal formula.
source_text: You will speak My words to them, if indeed they listen or are terrified, for it is an embittering house.

target_units.text: Thus said the Lord: Stand in the courtyard of the Lord’s house and deliver an oracle to all the Judeans and all who come to bow down in the Lord’s house—all the words I commanded you to deliver to them. Do not take away a word.
Perhaps they will hear and turn, each from his evil way, and I will cease from the evils I plan to do to them because of their evil practices.

relationship: command to eat answered by the prophet's obedience
rationale: Ezekiel is told to open his mouth and eat what he is given instead of becoming embittering. The following chapter identifies the food as the scroll and records his opened mouth and being fed it, the particular enactment of this instruction.
source_text: And you, son of man, hear the One speaking to you. Do not become embittering like the embittering house. Open your mouth wide and eat what I give you.”

target_units.text: He said to me, “Son of man, eat this scroll, then go and speak to the sons of Israel.”
I opened my mouth wide, and He fed me the scroll.

relationship: presented scroll subsequently commanded as food
rationale: Ezekiel sees a hand stretched toward him with a scroll. Ezekiel 3 then commands him to eat the roll before addressing Israel and describes his being fed it and tasting its sweetness, following the use of this particular presented object.
source_text: I looked, and behold, a hand was stretched toward me, and in it was a scroll of a book;

target_units.text: He said to me, “Son of man, eat this scroll, then go and speak to the sons of Israel.”
I opened my mouth wide, and He fed me the scroll.
He said to me, “Son of man, your mouth will eat, and your belly will be filled with this scroll that has been given to you.” I ate it, and in my mouth it became like sweet honey.

relationship: shared writing on both sides of its material
rationale: Ezekiel's scroll is written on back and front with lament, song and woe. Exodus likewise describes God's writing on both sides of the testimony tablets; the medium and contents differ, while the unusual two-sided inscription corresponds.
source_text: and He unrolled it before me. It had writing on the back and the front, and upon it were written a lament, a song and woe.

target_units.text: Moses turned and came down the mountain with the two tablets of the testimony in his hands, stone tablets written on both sides, on the one side and the other.
The tablets were God’s work, and the writing was God’s writing, engraved on the tablets.

relationship: identification of the scroll commanded as food
rationale: Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll before speaking to Israel. The preceding vision has shown the extended hand and unrolled, two-sided scroll bearing lament, song and woe, identifying the particular object now given as food.
source_text: He said to me, “Son of man, eat this scroll, then go and speak to the sons of Israel.”

target_units.text: I looked, and behold, a hand was stretched toward me, and in it was a scroll of a book;
and He unrolled it before me. It had writing on the back and the front, and upon it were written a lament, a song and woe.

relationship: the prophet's opened mouth answers the eating command
rationale: Ezekiel opens his mouth and is fed the scroll. This enacts the earlier command to open his mouth and eat what is given, in contrast with becoming embittering like the people.
source_text: I opened my mouth wide, and He fed me the scroll.

target_units.text: And you, son of man, hear the One speaking to you. Do not become embittering like the embittering house. Open your mouth wide and eat what I give you.”

relationship: shared sweetness of divine sayings compared with honey
rationale: The scroll given to fill Ezekiel's belly tastes like honey in his mouth. The psalm likewise calls God's sayings sweeter than honey and honeycomb to the mouth, applying the food comparison to divine speech rather than reporting a swallowed scroll.
source_text: He said to me, “Son of man, your mouth will eat, and your belly will be filled with this scroll that has been given to you.” I ate it, and in my mouth it became like sweet honey.

target_units.text: How sweet are Thy sayings to my throat, beyond honey and honeycomb to my mouth!

relationship: parallel sending to speak the words God commands
rationale: Ezekiel must go to Israel's house and speak God's words to them. Jeremiah likewise must go to everyone to whom God sends him and speak everything commanded, establishing the speaker's commission and the message's source.
source_text: He said to me, “Son of man, go, enter the house of Israel, and speak My words to them;

target_units.text: The Lord said to me, Do not say, I am young, because you will go to everyone to whom I send you, and you will speak according to everything I command you.

relationship: same-chapter explanation of the difficult speech Ezekiel is not sent to
rationale: Ezekiel is sent to Israel rather than a people of deep or heavy speech. The next unit develops that distinction as many peoples whose speech he would not understand, adding that they would listen if he were sent to them.
source_text: for you are not sent out to a people of deep speech and heavy tongue, but to the house of Israel,

target_units.text: nor to many peoples of foreign speech or foreign tongues, nor those strong in tongue whose words you will not understand. If I had sent you to such people, they would have listened to you.

relationship: related contrast between foreign response and resistant hearers
rationale: Ezekiel is told that peoples of unintelligible speech would listen if he were sent to them, before Israel's refusal is stated. Jesus likewise contrasts Nineveh's actual repentance at Jonah's preaching with the generation before Him; this is a counterpart in responsiveness, not an identification of the foreign peoples.
source_text: nor to many peoples of foreign speech or foreign tongues, nor those strong in tongue whose words you will not understand. If I had sent you to such people, they would have listened to you.

target_units.text: Men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at Jonah’s proclamation; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.

relationship: parallel rejection of God's messenger as rejection of God
rationale: Israel's house will not listen to Ezekiel because it will not listen to God. God likewise explains to Samuel that the people's treatment concerns His own rejected rule, and links their behavior toward Samuel with their longstanding abandonment of Him.
source_text: But the house of Israel certainly will not be willing to listen to you, because they do not wish to listen to Me; the entire house of Israel is contentious and hard-hearted.

target_units.text: The Lord said to Samuel, “Listen to the people’s voice in whatever they say to you. They have treated Me as nothing so that I should not reign over them; it is not you they have treated as nothing.
As in all the deeds they have done to Me from the day I brought them up from Egypt until this day, forsaking Me and serving other gods, so they are doing to you as well.

relationship: parallel strengthening of a prophet against hostile opponents
rationale: God strengthens Ezekiel's face and contention against those who resist him. Jeremiah is similarly made like a fortified city and strong bronze wall against rulers and people who will fight him, using different images for strength to withstand opposition.
source_text: Behold, I have made your face strong against their faces, and I will strengthen your contention against their contention,

target_units.text: Behold, on this day I have made you like a fortified city and like a strong bronze wall against all Judah’s kings, its rulers and the people of the land,
and they will fight you, but they will certainly not prevail against you, because I am with you to rescue you, said the Lord.

relationship: shared rock imagery for steadfastness without fear or shame
rationale: Following the strengthening language of 3:8, God says that it will always be stronger than rock and forbids fear of the opponents' faces. Isaiah's speaker likewise sets his face like solid rock because the Lord helps him and he will not be ashamed; the comparison does not substitute a forehead or diamond into Ezekiel.
source_text: and it will always be stronger than rock. Do not fear them or be terrified before their faces, for it is an embittering house.”

target_units.text: The Lord became my helper; therefore I was not abashed. Instead, I set my face like solid rock and knew that I would certainly not be ashamed.

relationship: parallel inward reception of divine words before speaking them
rationale: Ezekiel must receive all God's words in his heart and hear them with his ears. Deuteronomy likewise places commanded words in heart and soul before directing their repeated teaching and speaking, linking inward attention with verbal transmission.
source_text: He said to me, “Son of man, take into your heart all the words that I have spoken with you, and hear with your ears,

target_units.text: And these words, which I command you this day, shall be in your heart and in your soul.
And you shall teach them to your sons, and speak of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk in the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

relationship: same-chapter command to address the captives followed by arrival among them
rationale: Ezekiel is sent into captivity to his own people with the Lord's words. Ezekiel 3:15 then records his entry among the captives by Chebar and seven days living among them, giving the concrete arrival rather than inventing a different place name or silence.
source_text: and go, enter the captivity, to the sons of your people; you will speak to them and say to them, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ if indeed they listen, if indeed they yield.”

target_units.text: I entered the captivity aloft and went around those dwelling by the River Chebar, those who were there; I sat there seven days, living among them.

relationship: related heavenly acclamation of the Lord's glory
rationale: As a spirit raises Ezekiel, he hears a great shaking and an acclamation blessing the Lord's glory from His place. Isaiah's seraphim likewise proclaim the Lord's holiness and earth-filling glory, with the lintel lifted at their voice; the settings' disturbances are described differently.
source_text: A spirit took me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great shaking: “Blessed be the Lord’s glory from His place!”

target_units.text: And one cried to another, saying: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord Sabaoth; all the earth is full of His glory.
And the lintel was lifted at the sound of their cry, and the house was filled with smoke.

relationship: repeated description of the creatures' wing sound
rationale: Ezekiel 3 describes the sound of fluttering wings, wheels and great shaking, using the wording that he saw the sound. Ezekiel 1 had described hearing the wings like much water, supplying the earlier audible feature without normalizing the later sensory wording.
source_text: I saw the sound of the living creatures’ wings fluttering one toward another, and the sound of the wheels adjoining them, and the sound of the shaking.

target_units.text: As they went, I heard the sound of their wings like the sound of much water; when they stood, their wings came to rest.

relationship: parallel lifting and transport by a spirit
rationale: Ezekiel is raised and taken up by the spirit, impelled by his spirit with the Lord's hand strong upon him. Ezekiel 8 likewise depicts a spirit lifting him between earth and heaven and bringing him in a vision to Jerusalem; the source does not add bitterness to this movement.
source_text: The spirit raised me and took me up. I went, impelled by my spirit, and the Lord’s hand came strongly upon me.

relationship: same-chapter arrival at the commanded destination among captives
rationale: Ezekiel enters among the captives and lives among the Chebar inhabitants for seven days. This supplies the destination previously commanded when he was sent into captivity to his people, without importing a statement that he sat silent.
source_text: I entered the captivity aloft and went around those dwelling by the River Chebar, those who were there; I sat there seven days, living among them.

target_units.text: and go, enter the captivity, to the sons of your people; you will speak to them and say to them, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ if indeed they listen, if indeed they yield.”

relationship: repeated appointment as Israel's watchman
rationale: Both passages appoint the son of man as watchman for Israel's house and say he will hear a word from God's mouth. Ezekiel 3:17 explicitly adds conveying the warning, which the later chapter develops in its following units.
source_text: “Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel. You will hear a word from My mouth and convey My warning to them.

target_units.text: And you, son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for Israel’s house, and you will hear a word from My mouth.

relationship: repeated blood responsibility for an unwarned lawless person
rationale: Both warnings distinguish the lawless person's death in wrongdoing from the watchman's additional responsibility when he fails to warn. In each, God requires the person's blood from the watchman's hand.
source_text: When I say to the lawless person, ‘You will surely be put to death,’ and you do not warn him or speak to warn the lawless person to turn from his ways so that he may live, that lawless person will die in his injustice; but I will require his blood from your hand.

target_units.text: When I say to the sinner, ‘You will surely be put to death,’ and you do not speak so that the impious man may guard himself from his way, that lawless man will die in his lawlessness, but I will require his blood from your hand.

relationship: related freedom from blood responsibility through full proclamation
rationale: Ezekiel is held responsible for blood when he withholds the warning that could call a lawless person back. Paul conversely declares himself clean from everyone's blood because he did not withhold God's whole purpose, connecting faithful proclamation with freedom from that liability.
source_text: When I say to the lawless person, ‘You will surely be put to death,’ and you do not warn him or speak to warn the lawless person to turn from his ways so that he may live, that lawless person will die in his injustice; but I will require his blood from your hand.

target_units.text: Therefore I testify to you this very day that I am clean from the blood of all,
for I did not hold back from declaring to you the whole purpose of God.

relationship: repeated distinction between a refused warning and the watchman's rescued life
rationale: Both passages say that a warned lawless person who does not turn dies in wrongdoing, while the messenger has rescued his own life. The watchman's responsibility is discharged by warning, without a guarantee that the hearer repents.
source_text: But if you warn the lawless person and he does not turn from his lawlessness and his way, that lawless person will die in his injustice, while you will rescue your life.

target_units.text: But if you forewarn the impious man of his way so that he may turn from it and he does not turn from his way, this man will die in his impiety, and you have rescued your own life.

relationship: parallel former righteousness not remembered after wrongdoing
rationale: Ezekiel 3 says the righteous person's former deeds are not remembered when he turns to injustice and dies, also addressing the watchman's failure. Ezekiel 33 likewise says prior righteous deeds will not be remembered if the person does lawlessness, without repeating the watchman's blood liability in that unit.
source_text: When a righteous person turns from his righteous deeds and commits a transgression, and I place torment before his face, he will die because you did not warn him. He will die in his sins, because the righteous deeds he did certainly will not be remembered, and I will require his blood from your hand.

target_units.text: When I speak to the righteous man—this one has trusted in his righteousness, yet commits lawlessness—none of his righteous deeds will ever be remembered. In the injustice he committed, in it he will die.

relationship: related saving of both the teacher and attentive hearer
rationale: A warning that keeps the righteous person from sin preserves that person's life and rescues the watchman's own life. First Timothy likewise links continued attention to oneself and the teaching with saving both oneself and one's hearers; the forms of instruction and situations differ.
source_text: But if you warn the righteous person not to sin, and he does not sin, the righteous person will surely live because you warned him; and you will rescue your own life.”

target_units.text: Pay attention to yourself and to the teaching; continue in them, for by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

relationship: repeated Lord's hand and revelation in the plain
rationale: The Lord's hand comes upon Ezekiel and he is directed to the plain for speech. Ezekiel 37 again begins with the Lord's hand, transport in spirit to a plain and a spoken question, there concerning the bones seen in it.
source_text: The Lord’s hand came upon me, and He said to me, “Rise and go out to the plain, and you will be spoken to there.”

target_units.text: The Lord’s hand came upon me. The Lord brought me out in spirit and set me in the middle of the plain, which was full of human bones.
He led me all around them, and behold, there were very many upon the plain’s surface, very dry.
He said to me, ‘Son of man, will these bones live?’ I said, ‘Lord, Thou knowest these things.’

relationship: explicit recurrence of the Chebar glory and prostration
rationale: Ezekiel sees the Lord's glory in the plain as in the Chebar vision and falls on his face. Ezekiel 1:28 provides that earlier sight of the glory and the same prostration, making the connection explicit in the source itself.
source_text: I rose and went out to the plain, and behold, the Lord’s glory stood there, like the vision and like the glory I had seen by the River Chebar; and I fall upon my face.

relationship: repeated spirit coming upon and setting Ezekiel on his feet
rationale: A spirit comes upon Ezekiel and sets him on his feet before the instruction to be shut inside his house. Ezekiel 2 likewise records a spirit coming upon him and raising him to his feet to hear speech.
source_text: A spirit came upon me and set me on my feet. He spoke to me and said to me, “Go, be shut inside your house.

relationship: related bonds restraining the prophet's movements
rationale: Ezekiel is warned that bonds will bind him so he cannot go out from among the people. Ezekiel 4 likewise announces bonds, there preventing him from turning from one side to the other until the days of confinement end; the restricted movements differ.

target_units.text: Behold, I have placed bonds upon you; do not turn from side to side until the days of your confinement are completed.

relationship: later release from the prophetic muteness
rationale: God binds Ezekiel's tongue so that he becomes mute and cannot rebuke the embittering house. Ezekiel 33 records the opening of his mouth around the survivor's arrival announcing Jerusalem's capture, after which it was no longer restrained.
source_text: I will bind your tongue, and you will become mute; you will not be a man rebuking them, for it is an embittering house.

target_units.text: In the twelfth year of our captivity, in the twelfth month, on the fifth of the month, the survivor from Jerusalem came to me, saying, “The city has been captured!”
The Lord’s hand came upon me in the evening before he arrived, and He opened my mouth until he came to me in the morning. Once my mouth was opened, it was no longer restrained.

relationship: related divinely opened mouth and restored prophetic speech
rationale: God says He will open Ezekiel's mouth when speaking to him, so that Ezekiel can proclaim the divine word. Ezekiel 24 later promises an opened mouth toward the survivor, speech and the end of being struck mute.
source_text: But when I speak to you, I will open your mouth, and you will say to them, ‘Thus says the Lord: Let the one who hears hear, and let the one who disobeys disobey,’ for it is an embittering house.”

target_units.text: on that day the survivor will come to you to announce it into your ears?

relationship: same-chapter drawn Jerusalem within the enacted siege sign
rationale: Ezekiel is told to draw Jerusalem on a brick. The iron-pan wall and enacted siege in verse 3 conclude with the explanation that this is a sign for Israel, interpreting the model city within the larger demonstration.

target_units.text: Take an iron pan and place it as an iron wall between you and the city. Prepare your face against it; it will be besieged, and you will besiege it. This is a sign for the sons of Israel.

relationship: enacted siege compared with Jerusalem's reported siege
rationale: Ezekiel is commanded to arrange siege defenses, camps and missile positions against the drawn Jerusalem. Kings reports Babylon's king camping against Jerusalem, building an enclosing wall and maintaining the siege; it does not repeat every feature of the model.

relationship: same-chapter explanation of the modeled city and siege
rationale: The iron pan becomes a wall between Ezekiel and the city while he enacts its siege as a sign. The opening instructions identify that city as the Jerusalem drawn on the brick and specify its surrounding siege works, making the sign's referent concrete.
source_text: Take an iron pan and place it as an iron wall between you and the city. Prepare your face against it; it will be besieged, and you will besiege it. This is a sign for the sons of Israel.

lay siege to it, build forward defenses against it, throw up a palisade against it, set camps against it, and arrange missile positions all around.

relationship: same-chapter complementary sides bearing Israel's and Judah's wrongs
rationale: Ezekiel's left-side action bears Israel's wrong for 150 days. The corresponding right-side action bears Judah's wrong for 40 days; the comparison preserves the native durations rather than replacing them with conventional totals.
source_text: Lie on your left side and place the injustices of the house of Israel upon it, according to the number of days—one hundred fifty—that you lie upon it; bear their injustices.

target_units.text: and complete all these things. Lie on your right side and bear the injustices of the house of Judah forty days. I have appointed you a day for a year.

relationship: same-chapter repeated 190-day duration of the enacted burden
rationale: God assigns 190 days for the two injustices and the bearing of Israel's wrong. The food instructions likewise specify 190 days of lying on the side, coordinating the enactment's duration with its provision without substituting another number.

relationship: shared day-for-year reckoning while bearing wrongdoing
rationale: Ezekiel bears Judah's wrong for 40 days with a day assigned for a year. Numbers likewise interprets the 40 days of searching the land as 40 years of bearing sin, explicitly using the day-for-year relation in a different judgment.
source_text: and complete all these things. Lie on your right side and bear the injustices of the house of Judah forty days. I have appointed you a day for a year.

target_units.text: According to the number of days you searched out the land—forty days, a day for a year—you shall bear your sins for forty years, and you shall know the fury of My anger.

relationship: related binding that prevents the prophet's movement
rationale: God's bonds prevent Ezekiel from turning sides until the confinement days end. The earlier warning likewise foretold binding, there restricting his going out from among the people rather than his turning during the sign.
source_text: Behold, I have placed bonds upon you; do not turn from side to side until the days of your confinement are completed.

target_units.text: And you, son of man, behold, bonds have been placed upon you, and they will bind you with them; you certainly will not go out from among them.

relationship: same-chapter food provision coordinated with the 190-day burden
rationale: The combined grains are made into bread to eat during 190 days on the side. Ezekiel 4:5 had specified the same 190 days for bearing Israel's wrong, connecting the unusual food provision to the stated duration.

rationale: Ezekiel's food is weighed at 20 shekels daily and eaten at intervals. The later interpretation says Jerusalem will eat bread by weight in need, identifying the ration's feature with the announced shortage without assigning the 20-shekel quantity to every resident.

rationale: Ezekiel is assigned a measured sixth of a hin to drink at intervals. Verse 16 interprets the sign with water drunk by measure and in devastation, linking the controlled water ration with the city's deprivation.

rationale: The barley cake is to be baked with human-dung pellets before the people's eyes. The next unit interprets the sign as Israel eating unclean things among the nations; it does not say the dung itself is the food.

relationship: parallel unclean food among foreign peoples
rationale: Ezekiel predicts Israel eating unclean things among the nations. Hosea likewise says that among the Assyrians they will eat unclean things and describes bread or sacrifices that defile their eaters, connecting life among foreign peoples with food impurity.

relationship: parallel protest of lifelong avoidance of unclean food
rationale: Ezekiel protests the eating instruction by affirming his lifelong avoidance of defiling foods. Peter likewise answers a command to eat by saying he has never eaten anything common and unclean; the subsequent divine responses differ.

A voice came to him again, a second time: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common.”

relationship: legal counterpart for meat from animals that died or were killed by beasts
rationale: Ezekiel specifically denies eating an animal that died on its own or was killed by beasts. Leviticus names those same sources of meat as making the eater unclean and prescribes washing, supplying a concrete food-law counterpart to his protest.
source_text: I said, “By no means, Lord, God of Israel! Behold, my life has not been defiled with uncleanness. From my birth until now I have eaten neither what died of itself nor what a wild animal killed, nor has any stale meat entered my mouth.”

rationale: God grants cattle dung for the bread in place of human-dung pellets. The preceding instruction and Ezekiel's protest supply the particular request and original fuel to which this concession responds.

relationship: parallel bread scarcity and weighed portions
rationale: Ezekiel announces broken support of bread and bread eaten by weight in need, alongside measured water. Leviticus likewise threatens bread scarcity, bread returned by weight and eating without fullness; it does not include the water clause.
source_text: He said to me, “Son of man, behold, I am breaking the support of bread in Jerusalem. They will eat bread by weight and in need, and drink water by measure and in devastation,

target_units.text: When I afflict you with a scarcity of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in one oven and give back your bread by weight. You shall eat and in no wise be filled.

relationship: parallel wasting away because of wrongdoing
rationale: Ezekiel says the lack of bread and water leads to wasting away in wrongdoings. Leviticus similarly predicts survivors being ruined because of their sins and wasting away in enemy territory, while not repeating Ezekiel's paired food and water shortage.
source_text: so that they become needy for bread and water. A man and his brother will disappear, and they will waste away in their injustices.

target_units.text: And those who remain of you shall be ruined because of your sins; they shall waste away in the land of their enemies.

relationship: shared shaving of head and beard as a judgment image
rationale: Ezekiel must use a sword sharper than a barber's razor upon his head and beard before dividing the hair. Isaiah likewise depicts the Lord shaving head and beard with a great and drunken razor associated with the Assyrians, adding the hair of the feet rather than the weighed portions.

relationship: same-chapter quartered hair and quartered judgments upon the people
rationale: The hair is divided into four quarters: two burned, one struck by sword and one scattered to wind, with a pursuing sword. The later explanation likewise uses four quarters for death, famine, scattering and sword; it does not reproduce the two fire actions as identical descriptions.
source_text: burn a quarter with fire inside the city when the days of siege are complete. Take a quarter and burn it up in its midst; cut down a quarter with the sword around it, and scatter a quarter to the wind. I will draw a sword after them.

target_units.text: A quarter of you will be consumed by death; a quarter of you will perish by famine within you; a quarter of you I will scatter to every wind; and a quarter of you will fall by the sword around you, and I will draw a sword after them.

relationship: same-chapter reserved hairs subjected to a further burning
rationale: A few hairs are gathered into Ezekiel's cloak. The next instruction takes some of these and burns them, showing why the reserved portion cannot simply be treated as an unqualified promise that every selected hair escapes judgment.
source_text: Take a few of them in number and gather them into your cloak.

target_units.text: Take some of these again, cast them into the fire, and burn them in the fire. From it fire will go out. And you will say to the entire house of Israel,

relationship: same-chapter antecedent of the hairs taken again for burning
rationale: The command to take some of these again and burn them follows the gathering of a few hairs into the cloak. That earlier instruction identifies the selected hairs now subjected to the further fire action.

relationship: related central placement of Jerusalem and gathered Israel
rationale: Jerusalem is placed amid the nations with lands around her. Ezekiel 38 describes a nation gathered from many nations dwelling upon the earth's navel; both portray a central position, while the target speaks of the gathered nation rather than explicitly naming Jerusalem.
source_text: ‘Thus says the Lord: This is Jerusalem. I have placed her amid the nations, and the lands around her.

target_units.text: to take plunder and strip their spoils, to turn your hand against the desolate land that was inhabited and against a nation gathered from many nations, acquiring possessions, dwelling upon the earth’s navel.

relationship: parallel proclamation of rejected divine law
rationale: Ezekiel is directed to speak God's ordinances and laws amid people who rejected them. Jeremiah likewise must proclaim the covenant words in Judah's cities and outside Jerusalem with a command to do them, followed by the statement that they did not do them.
source_text: And you will speak My ordinances to the lawless one among the nations, and My laws among the lands around her; for they rejected My ordinances and did not walk in My laws.

relationship: related indictment against the standard of surrounding nations
rationale: Jerusalem has not kept God's ordinances or even acted according to the surrounding nations' ordinances. Kings likewise indicts the people led astray by Manasseh as doing evil beyond the nations, retaining its comparative language rather than making the two accusations identical.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: Because your impulse comes from the nations around you, and you have not walked in My laws or performed My ordinances—nor have you even acted according to the ordinances of the nations around you—

relationship: parallel God acting against Jerusalem in judgment
rationale: God declares Himself against Jerusalem and promises judgment in her midst before the nations. source_text: therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I am against you, and I will execute judgment in your midst before the nations,

And I will strike all this city’s inhabitants, the people and the livestock, with a great death, and they will die.

relationship: parallel unprecedented calamity upon Jerusalem
rationale: God threatens Jerusalem with acts unlike what He has done before or will do again because of its abominations. Daniel likewise confesses calamities in Jerusalem unlike those that had occurred under heaven, without repeating Ezekiel's additional statement about the future.
source_text: and I will do among you what I have not done and the like of which I will not do again, according to all your abominations.

target_units.text: He established for us His commands, all He spoke against us and against our judges, all Thou didst judge for us, bringing great calamities upon us, such as had not occurred under heaven as occurred in Jerusalem.

relationship: shared judgment of parents eating their children
rationale: Ezekiel predicts fathers eating children and children eating fathers. Leviticus likewise warns of eating sons' and daughters' flesh, supporting the parent-to-child part without supplying Ezekiel's reverse direction.
source_text: Therefore fathers will eat children in your midst, and children will eat fathers. I will execute judgments against you and scatter all your survivors to every wind.

target_units.text: And you shall eat the flesh of your sons, and the flesh of your daughters you shall eat.

relationship: parallel divine scattering of the people
rationale: Beyond the cannibalism warning, Ezekiel predicts scattering all survivors to every wind. Leviticus likewise threatens scattering among nations and an advancing sword, a distinct counterpart to this dispersal clause rather than the family violence.
source_text: Therefore fathers will eat children in your midst, and children will eat fathers. I will execute judgments against you and scatter all your survivors to every wind.

rationale: Ezekiel grounds God's rejection and refusal of mercy in the defilement of His holy places by abominations. Jeremiah likewise identifies Judah's placing abominations in the house bearing God's name as defiling it, supplying the same concrete cultic offense.

relationship: same-chapter four population portions explaining the divided hair
rationale: Death, famine, scattering and sword divide the people into four quarters. The earlier hair sign likewise divides into four quarters, with two burnings, sword and wind; the connection keeps the sign's actions distinct from the explanation's named calamities.

target_units.text: burn a quarter with fire inside the city when the days of siege are complete. Take a quarter and burn it up in its midst; cut down a quarter with the sword around it, and scatter a quarter to the wind. I will draw a sword after them.

relationship: parallel jealousy and wrath in response to faithlessness
rationale: Ezekiel says the completed anger will show that the Lord spoke in jealousy. Deuteronomy likewise explicitly joins God's jealousy and wrath to provocation by idols, with fire arising from that wrath; it does not repeat Ezekiel's recognition formula.

rationale: Ezekiel announces Jerusalem and her surrounding daughters becoming wilderness before every passerby. Jeremiah likewise announces the city becoming a ruin that every passerby observes, adding their gloomy looks and hissing rather than repeating the daughters clause.

rationale: Jerusalem will be mourned and ravaged among surrounding nations when God judges her. Jeremiah likewise describes the ruined city with passersby looking gloomy and hissing over its wound; the shared ruin and onlookers' response preserve the different expressions of grief or reaction.
source_text: you will be mourned and ravaged among the nations around you when I execute judgments against you in the vengeance of My wrath. I, the Lord, have spoken.

relationship: shared divine arrows and wasting through hunger
rationale: Ezekiel calls famine God's arrows, bringing exhaustion and breaking the bread supply. Deuteronomy likewise joins God's spent arrows with wasting away in hunger, while also adding birds, spasms and wild creatures.

rationale: Ezekiel exposes each elder's hidden bedchamber and the claim that God does not see. Isaiah likewise condemns secret counsel and deeds in darkness whose practitioners ask who has seen or knows them, specifically paralleling the concealment that accompanies the false confidence.
source_text: He said to me, “Son of man, have you seen what the elders of the house of Israel do, each in their hidden bedchamber? For they said, ‘The Lord does not see; the Lord has abandoned the land.’”

target_units.text: Woe to those making deep counsel, but not through the Lord! Woe to those making counsel in secret! Their deeds will be in darkness, and they will say, “Who has seen us, and who will know us or what we do?”
